questions.q: The HPA scales checkout from 3 to 25 replicas, but there's no node with enough free capacity for the new Pods. What happens to those Pods?
options: They are automatically deleted by the scheduler
They sit in Pending status, with a FailedScheduling event citing insufficient CPU/memory
They are forcibly placed on an overloaded node anyway
The HPA automatically reduces its own target replica count
questions.explain: When no node has enough free capacity, new Pods remain Pending, and kubectl describe shows a FailedScheduling event citing insufficient resources — exactly the signal the Cluster Autoscaler watches for.

questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between what the HPA scales and what the Cluster Autoscaler scales?
options: Both scale the same thing — replica count — but on different schedules
The HPA scales Pod replica count on a Deployment; the Cluster Autoscaler scales node count on a cloud-provider node group
The HPA scales nodes; the Cluster Autoscaler scales Pods
The Cluster Autoscaler only works on bare-metal clusters, never in the cloud
questions.explain: HPA adjusts the number of Pod replicas for a workload. Cluster Autoscaler adjusts the number of nodes in a node group (ASG, VM Scale Set, node pool) to provide capacity for those Pods.

questions.q: Why is Cluster Autoscaler scale-down generally more conservative than scale-up?
options: Scale-down requires manual approval in every case
Removing a node safely requires confirming its Pods can be relocated elsewhere, and certain Pods (local storage, bare Pods, eviction-blocked) can prevent removal entirely
Scale-down is actually faster and less careful than scale-up
Cluster Autoscaler never performs scale-down automatically
questions.explain: Scale-down involves safety checks: a node is only removed if its workloads can be relocated, and certain Pod types (using local storage, lacking a controller, or annotated against eviction) block the node from being removed.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct example of how Cluster Autoscaler integrates with a cloud provider?
options: It directly edits the Kubernetes binary on each node
On AWS it drives an Auto Scaling Group; on Azure a VM Scale Set; on GKE a managed node pool
It only works by physically racking new servers
It bypasses the cloud provider entirely and creates nodes from nothing
questions.explain: Cluster Autoscaler is cloud-provider-specific and drives that provider's node-group construct — an AWS ASG, Azure VM Scale Set, or GKE managed node pool — to add or remove actual nodes.

questions.q: How do the HPA and Cluster Autoscaler typically cooperate during a traffic spike, without directly knowing about each other?
options: The Cluster Autoscaler must be manually triggered after the HPA scales up
The HPA reacts first to a rising metric and requests more replicas; if existing nodes lack room, those Pods go Pending, which the Cluster Autoscaler then reacts to by adding node capacity
They operate on a shared, synchronized schedule set by the cluster administrator
The HPA calls the Cluster Autoscaler's API directly to request new nodes
questions.explain: The two controllers act independently on different signals — the HPA on metrics, the Cluster Autoscaler on Pending Pods — but their effects naturally chain together: HPA creates demand, Cluster Autoscaler supplies the capacity if needed.
